newsitem.title: TURKEY: FEATURE - Turks grapple with bureaucratic machine.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Turks grapple with bureaucratic machine.

text.p: Yasar Yasamaz cannot have an identity card because he is listed as having died in World War One and also in Turkey's 1919 war of independence -- both on dates before he was born.

In a popular book about the ultimate bureaucratic nightmare by the late satirist Aziz Nesin, Yasar's lack of an identity card prevents him from going to school, getting married or claiming his inheritance, but he is still called up for military service and is liable for his father's debts.
Turks like the book because it rings so true.
"There are lots of Yasar Yasamaz cases here. This is Turkey -- anything goes," said Ali Erdem, head of the records office in the Turkish resort town of Kusadasi.
"There are people recorded as dead when they are alive, alive when they are dead, male when they are female," he said.
In a country where an identity card is indispensable even for the simplest of operations, this is a serious problem.
And setting the record straight pits you against Turkey's formidable bureaucratic machine.
RIGHTING WRONGS

Cetin Kaya Arslan, a 59-year-old former leather worker, was shocked to find that he could not claim his inheritance after the death of his only surviving relative because his grandmother -- who died decades ago -- was still registered as alive.
"My grandmother's nephew died and because he was unmarried the inheritance came back to me," Arslan told Reuters.

"But when I went to make my claim I was startled to see she was 'alive'. I told the clerk: 'Oh, just rub her out then.' But he said you couldn't kill someone off like that. I said: 'But she's already dead.' He was unimpressed," Arslan lamented.

Arslan had to find two very old men to testify she was dead and apply to the local governor, who sent the application to the police station, who sent it to the district headman, who sent it to the police chief, who finally sent it to the records office.

He got off lightly because it turned out that the district headman had forgotten to pass on his grandmother's death certificate to the record offices. If the original certificate had been wrong or missing he would have had to sue, and Turkish court cases normally take months or years.

Erdem said mistakes often happen because civil servants are stretched with the endless fiddly work writing down records in huge black volumes. Also, documents can get misdirected or lost in Turkey's lumbering postal service, and some officials destroy them because it is nothing to do with their district.
"IGNORANT" HEADMEN
But a main player in all this is the village or district headman, who can be "ignorant and irresponsible", Erdem said.

"People often find they can't find the headman as he is off in a field somewhere," he said. "In Kusadasi (with a population of 20,000) I can show you over 100 people 'living' at over 150 years for such reasons. And some headmen are ignorant and can easily be swayed to fiddle with records."
Kemal Yildir, a former military officer and late mayor of Kusadasi, faced a similar but more traumatic problem.

"The mayor's son found when he got married that the family name was registered wrongly, as Cildir. While trying to sort this out we found that the mayor was dead -- well, officially. He had apparently died in 1938," Erdem said.
Yildir, who served as Kusadasi mayor in the early 1980s, had to go to court to prove he was alive. He died a few years later.
Erdem, who was a close friend of Yildir, said the headman in the village where Yildir was born had decided his long absence meant he was dead and prepared a death certificate accordingly.
WOMEN CALLED UP TO THE ARMY
It is also common for women to be erroneously registered as men at birth and later called up for military service. Sometimes they even have to get a doctor's certificate to prove their sex.
"They called me up. Then seeing I was not a man, they said I had better get an official document proving I was female or I would be obliged to go into the army," said Nese Karaahmet, 21.
A recent issue of the Official Gazette shows a man seriously caught up in the bureaucratic mangle.
'K.Z.' applied in 1992 to correct the record books, which had his dead wife alive and single and their son illegitimate.

In 1993, the court that first heard the case decided it was the wrong place to decide the matter and passed it on to another, which washed its hands of the affair last June. In October, a higher court decided that the original court in Hatay in southern Turkey should have heard the case, sending 'K.Z.' back to square one.
Nesin's story ends when Yasar, in prison for causing a riot in frustration while dealing with obstructive council clerks, takes up organised crime as the only way to get things done.
In real life, too, criminals can gain from the system.
In a famous case in Kusadasi, a man convicted on capital charges could not be hanged because he had no identity card and police could not find any record of his existence.

And because identity cards are often the be-all and end-all, if you can forge someone else's ID you can sell his house. Again, Erdem said this had happened in Kusadasi and a landowner came back from living abroad to find his property sold.
